Explanatory Notes

  1. This report is the v1 Precision Report of the §35 'National Capacity Index' engine on the website. It is an engine created with a different meaning from the Country Analysis (Λ¹²), and its measurement target is the capacity of institutional policies to reach the grassroots stratum(Cheonghae definition, 2026-10-17).
  2. Formulas, weights, and normalization follow Cheonghae approval (2026-10-17). All figures are calculated by program from original public data values; no figures are handwritten. Original values are as published, and missing values are left as missing.
  3. The population consists of 197 countries in the Country Analysis Series (2026-10-07). 11 countries with fewer than 3 valid axes were not computed.
  4. Narratives range from Layer 1 (data) to Layer 5 (interpretation based on prior research) of the six-layer discourse. Prescriptions, moral evaluations, leader assessments, and predictions are not made.

Prologue — What Does It Measure?

The capacity of a state is often measured in aggregate terms such as administrative efficiency, rule of law, or finance. This engine changes the question. It does not measure whether policies were created, but whether those policies actually reached the most marginalized people. Two countries with the same social security system can have vastly different rates of benefit uptake among the bottom 20%, the proportion of households bankrupted by medical expenses, the proportion of poor children completing middle school, and the extent to which taxes and transfers actually reduce disparities.

The BSLI in the Country Analysis Series measures the clothing, food, and housing pressure received by the grassroots stratum (30th–50th income percentiles). The National Capacity Index measures the degree to which policies reach that grassroots stratum. When overlapped, countries with high pressure but no policy reach, or in other words, policy gaps, appear (Part 5).

Part 1 Formulas and Indicators

NCI v1 = 0.25·R1 + 0.25·R2 + 0.25·R3 + 0.25·R4   (Rᵢ ∈ [0,1], valid axes ≥ 3)

Each axis score is the mean of the normalized values of the indicators on that axis. Normalization uses Min-Max as in Country Analysis Series §1.5, anchoring on the minimum and maximum among 197 countries with available values (X* = (X − min)/(max − min), reverse indicators are 1 − X*). Weights were set equally to preclude arbitrary adjustment.

AxisIndicator (as published)DirectionCountries with ValuesAnchor (Min–Max)
R1Social protection and labor program uptake rate among the bottom 20% (%) — ASPIREPositive direction1100.490244 ~ 99.3397
R1Share of population receiving at least one social protection benefit (%) — SDG 1.3.1(ILO)Positive direction1920 ~ 100
R2UHC service coverage index — SDG 3.8.1(WHO)Positive direction19326 ~ 92
R2Share of population spending more than 10% of household budget on healthcare (%) — SDG 3.8.2(WHO), reverse directionReverse1430.13 ~ 35.53
R3Share of bottom 40% with a financial account (%) — FindexPositive direction1556.50494 ~ 100
R3Middle school completion equity index (poorest÷richest, adjusted) — SDG 4.5.1(UIS)Positive direction1210.03152 ~ 1.02222
R4Redistributive reach rate (%) = (Market Gini − Disposable Gini)/Market Gini — SWIIDPositive direction178-13.07 ~ 47.61

Classification: Strong Reach (NCI > 0.7) · Moderate Reach (0.4–0.7) · Weak Reach (0.2–0.4) · Reach Gap (< 0.2). Classification boundaries follow the existing boundaries on the website §35.

Part 2 Data and Missing Values

The number of countries reporting for each indicator varies. The social protection uptake rate (ASPIRE) is mainly surveyed in middle- and low-income countries, leaving many high-income countries blank, and R1 for those countries is populated only by SDG 1.3.1 (ILO). The education equity index (SDG 4.5.1) is also limited to countries with household surveys. Each indicator reflects the most recent observation year available for each country (2010 or later), and years vary by country.

Countries not computed (11 countries): Antigua and Barbuda, Brunei Darussalam, Republic of Cuba, State of Eritrea, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Liechtenstein, Macao, Monaco, Democratic People's Republic of Korea, Syrian Arab Republic, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.

Part 3 Results

Classification distribution among 186 computed countries: Strong Reach 53 countries · Moderate Reach 81 countries · Weak Reach 46 countries · Reach Gap 6 countries.

Part 4 Verification

Independence — Correlation with Country Analysis Series Indicators

The standard of Axiom A0 (if the correlation r between two indices is > 0.95, they are not independent and meaningless) was applied as is.

Comparison TargetnPearson rSpearman ρAssessment
η (Series)1860.6300.572Satisfies independence criterion (r ≤ 0.95)
BSLI (Series)1380.8400.861Satisfies independence criterion (r ≤ 0.95)
A2 Institutional Trust1850.6950.670Satisfies independence criterion (r ≤ 0.95)
A8 Governance1850.7670.745Satisfies independence criterion (r ≤ 0.95)

The correlation with BSLI is the highest. This indicates that policy reach and grassroots living pressure move strongly together, and since it falls within the threshold (0.95), the two indices are believed to measure different things. The quadrant in Part 5 represents cases where the two diverge in the same country.

Sensitivity — How much the ranking is maintained when one axis is removed

Removed AxisnSpearman ρ with Original Ranking
R1 Income Security Reach1860.972

Comparison with Uprising Compendium Data

Comparison ItemnSpearman ρ
Number of Coup Attempts (1950–)186-0.577
Number of Years with MM Protests (1990–2020)186-0.049

Countries with frequent coup attempts have lower policy reach (negative correlation). It has almost no relation to the number of years protests were recorded — protest data rely on media reports, which are more likely to be captured in countries with freer press access (Uprising Compendium Vol. 1 Part 4).

Falsification Conditions

  1. If the social protection take-up rate of the bottom 20% is observed to remain persistently below 30% in 'reach robust' countries, the R1 definition is rejected.
  2. If the correlation between NCI and BSLI exceeds 0.95 in a subsequent update, the assumption of independence of the two indices is rejected.
  3. If the rank correlation drops below 0.8 when one axis is removed, it is considered that the index is dominated by a single axis, and the weights are re-examined.

Part 5 Policy Gap Quadrant

The horizontal axis is the BSLI from the Country Analysis Series (the more negative, the greater the grassroots suffering; Axiom A10), and the vertical axis is NCI. The baseline is the median of 138 countries with both values (BSLI -0.1324, NCI 0.5687).

Q4 (High Pressure · Low Reach) is the 'policy void' zone where the grassroots face significant pressure but policy does not reach them. Q3 is a zone of high pressure with relatively high policy reach, and Q2 is a zone of low pressure with low policy reach. The quadrants record position, not judgment.

Representative Policy — Bolsa Família — Conditional cash transfer based on the Unified Registry (CadÚnico)

According to an MDS announcement, in June 2026, Bolsa Família was disbursed to 19.34 million households with a monthly expenditure of R$ 13.08 billion. In the same report, approximately 2.26 million households were counted as eligible for the 'protection rule' (average R$ 369.27).

According to the IBGE PNAD survey (reported by Agência Brasil), in 2025, 17.2% of all households (13.6 million households) received Bolsa Família, and the proportion of households benefiting from all federal social programs was 22.7%. Regional disparities were large: 39.8% in the Northeast and 38.8% in the North compared to 10.8% in the South, and the average monthly income per beneficiary household was R$ 886, about one-third of that of non-beneficiary households (R$ 2,787).

According to an interim evaluation report published by the International Security and Development Center (ISDC) in June 2026 with support from a joint World Bank–UNHCR data center, the Lisungi program began as a pilot cash transfer for the poorest households funded by the World Bank in 2014, expanded to livelihood support in 2019, and then to Likouala Department in 2020 using refugee and host community funding. The Likouala design involved conditional cash transfers to 4,000 households of Bantus, Pygmies, and refugees and livelihood support for 8,000 households, with quarterly disbursements ranging from 10,000 to 135,000 FCFA. In surveys from 2021 to 2023, the adult-equivalent daily consumption of beneficiary households increased by an average of 157 FCFA (25% of the daily consumption of one adult), and the Lisungi transfer amounted to 65% of annual consumption for beneficiary households, reaching up to 200% in the lowest quintile and 20% in the highest quintile. The effects were larger among host communities than among refugees.

Representative Policy — Targeted cash transfer Renta Ciudadana based on Sisbén IV (replacing Familias en Acción in 2024) and the tax-and-transfer redistribution system

The Ministry of Social Prosperity (DPS) implemented the first cycle of Renta Ciudadana payments from April 30 to May 17, 2024, reaching 519,408 households. The program consists of four lines: 'Recognition of Care Value' targeting Sisbén IV A-class (extreme poverty) households with barriers to income generation; 'Colombia without Hunger' for extreme poverty households; 'Capacity Building' for B-class (moderate poverty) households; and disaster response. The 'Colombia without Hunger' amount is up to 500,000 pesos every 45 days. DPS stated that if demand exceeds supply, it will prioritize based on socioeconomic conditions and household composition, and expand gradually according to the medium-term fiscal plan.

The authors described the redistributive effect as smaller than in OECD countries, the tax system as progressive but insufficiently so because many high-income households do not pay actual taxes, indirect taxes such as VAT as regressive, and room for improving targeting of cash transfers and subsidies.

On February 6, 2023, the World Bank approved $30 million in grant aid for Comoros' 'Shock-Responsive and Resilience Social Safety Net Project,' of which $15 million was earmarked for the crisis response window. The project targets approximately 40,000 households and about 200,000 people across 200 villages on three islands, representing approximately 26% of Comoros' population and 32% of the population in the project area. This impact was reported to be particularly concentrated among low-income households.

According to the WHO Results Report country case, the WHO 2021 analysis identified out-of-pocket spending on outpatient medications and inpatient care, hospitals' balance billing, inadequate pharmaceutical price regulation, public coverage caps, and a lack of service volume control mechanisms as factors driving catastrophic healthcare costs. Subsequently, in late 2022–early 2023, the reference pricing system for over 2,300 medications and the introduction of DRGs led to the abolition of hospital balance billing, and the Georgian government announced that the proportion of patient out-of-pocket spending on inpatient care had fallen from 27% in 2022 to 10% in 2023. The same source indicated that the share of out-of-pocket spending fell from 73% in 2012 to 40% in 2022 (pre-reform figures).

Representative Policy — Guaranteed Minimum Benefit (zajamčena minimalna naknada, ZMN) and local government housing cost support for income security of the lowest stratum

According to the Croatian Government Administrative Portal guide, the guaranteed minimum benefit is paid as a certain percentage of the annual amount (osnovica) set by the government each year; the page indicates the base amount as 150 euros. A single-person household with work capacity receives 100% of the base amount (150 euros), an elderly or fully incapacitated single-person household receives 130% (195 euros), and household members are combined at 70% for adults and 70% for children; if a household has income, the amount paid is the guaranteed amount minus monthly income. Local governments are required to provide at least 30% of the guaranteed amount toward housing costs.

According to a joint report by the World Health Organization, the Ministry of Health, and the General Statistics Department (2023), the combined coverage rate of all social health protection schemes was 94%, but in the 2018/2019 household expenditure survey, only 16.1% of respondents reported having health insurance, and NHI awareness was lowest among the lower consumption quintiles and rural residents.

According to the same report, the rate of catastrophic medical expenses, defined as out-of-pocket medical expenses exceeding 10% of household budgets, was 4.2% in 2007/2008, 6.8% in 2012/2013, and 4.1% in 2018/2019. The proportion of the population receiving care when sick increased from 21% to 36% over the same period.

The CEQ study (Arunatilake, Inchauste & Lustig, 2017), using the 2009/10 household survey data, found that Sri Lanka's tax and social spending were overall redistributive and reduced poverty, but the effect was minimal due to low tax revenue and constrained fiscal capacity, resulting in a small scale of social spending. Direct transfers showed strong progressivity, while in-kind transfers for education and health had equalizing effects; however, a substantial portion of the increased indirect subsidies went to non-poor households. The redistribution reach of the raw index value (SWIID) was -12.09 (2019), recording a higher Gini after taxes and transfers.

Representative Policy — Cash transfers funded by donor agencies such as Fiavota and Toseke Boni Aigui, and health budget — Focused on responding to the southern drought

According to the World Bank (2022-10-31), social protection in Madagascar covers only about 6% of the extremely poor, and public spending on social safety nets amounts to 0.3% of GDP, falling short of the regional average of 1.2% for Sub-Saharan Africa. In 2021, government funding accounted for 16% of social safety net programs, with the remainder largely borne by development cooperation agencies.

According to the same World Bank data, the cash transfer program Fiavota, which began in response to the 2016 southern drought, reached approximately 430,000 people across 37 communes, and Toseke Boni Aigui, launched in 2021, supported 320,000 people in the 20 most affected communes. Both programs were designed as local and crisis-response initiatives.

Representative Policy — Elderly Basic Pension (universal pension without contributions) and Husnuvaa Aasandha (universal health insurance)

According to a HelpAge International–UNFPA case study (2022), the Maldives introduced an unconditional old-age basic pension and a contributory retirement pension in 2010 following the enactment of the Pension Act in 2009. The basic pension is available to citizens aged 65 or older whose other pension income does not exceed twice the basic pension; in 2020, an average of 18,139 people received it per month, with annual disbursements totaling MVR 1.03 billion. As of March 2019, the basic pension amount was MVR 5,000 per month. The contributory retirement pension applies to all public sector workers and more than 70% of private sector employees but is voluntary for informal sector workers.

UNICEF's interim evaluation reported that poverty rates were 11%p lower and extreme poverty rates 9%p lower in households whose support continued compared to those whose support was discontinued, while it described that households whose per capita daily consumption had been 0.32 dollars before the intervention remained below the international poverty line (3 dollars) even if their consumption tripled.

Philip Alston, UN Special Rapporteur on extreme poverty and human rights, noted in his August 2019 statement concluding his visit that the official poverty rate, which fell from 49% in 1970 to 0.4% in 2016, was based on a poverty line (about $234 per month for a four-person household) that had remained virtually fixed for decades, and that independent analyses indicated the actual poverty rate was around 15%. He requested that stateless households, migrant workers, and refugees be included in the statistics. Subsequently, the government revised the poverty line and recalculated the 2019 absolute poverty rate at 5.6%.

According to the World Bank's 2025 impact summary of the Sahel Adaptive Social Protection Program (PPSAS), the Wadata Talaka social safety net provided 15,000 CFA francs per month (approximately 10,000 CFA francs at the time of evaluation, about 15% of the 2015 rural poverty line) to women recipients in poor households selected through proxy income surveys for two years, expanding to approximately 190,000 households (about 1.65 million people) between 2012 and 2023. According to a study combining administrative fiscal data from the same period as the 2015 'Listening to Tajikistan' household survey using the Fairness Commitment (CEQ) methodology, the tax and transfer system raised the poverty rate at the $3.20/day (PPP) line by 5.12 percentage points. According to a WHO European Regional Office analysis of financial protection (2024), 18% of Tajikistan households faced catastrophic health expenditures in 2022, the highest level in Europe and Central Asia. Catastrophic health expenditures were consistently highest among the bottom 5 income quintiles, with out-of-pocket costs for outpatient medications being the main driver. Out-of-pocket spending accounted for 64% of current health expenditure in 2021, public health spending was 2% of GDP (7% of the government budget), and in 2018, 47% of health facility revenue came from informal and other direct payments and 6% from official out-of-pocket payments. The national coverage package imposes an 80% copayment for specialist care outside specific social, age, and disability criteria and excludes outpatient prescription medications and diagnostic tests.

According to a fiscal attribution analysis by the Asian Development Bank (ADB) applying the Fairness Commitment (CEQ) methodology to the 2014 Living Standards Survey (TLSLS 2014/15) and government administrative data (April 2024), the Gini coefficient declined from 0.320 in market income to 0.289 in total income and 0.270 in final income. Cash and near-cash transfers reduced the Gini by 3.1 percentage points, while in-kind health and education benefits reduced it by 1.6 percentage points; the effects of direct taxes, indirect taxes, and subsidies were negligible. In the same analysis, the poverty rate under the national poverty line (556.5 USD per capita in 2014) fell from 51.7% on market income to 29.9% on final income, a decline of 21.8 percentage points; the report noted that this was smaller than the average Gini reduction across 31 countries applying CEQ (8.3 percentage points), but larger by about 2 percentage points than the projection based on per capita income levels.

IRG revenue declined by 30% year on year, delaying civil servant salary payments, and as of September 2025 only 19% of the UN humanitarian response plan's $2.5 billion requirement had been mobilized. More than 60% of households in both IRG- and Houthi-controlled areas reported insufficient food consumption.

Representative Policy — Social Cash Transfer (SCT) — Mixed targeting combining MCDSS categories and proxy asset indices

According to a statement by Minister Doreen Mwamba of the Ministry of Community Development and Social Services (MCDSS) reported on February 20, 2026, SCT beneficiary households increased from 1.3 million to 1,555,840. The 2025 new enrollment plan was for 250,000 households, but more than 300,000 (new enrollments: 305,000) were actually added, and the February–March 2026 disbursements began on February 20 targeting more than 1.5 million households over 4 weeks.

The central evaluation by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (Sida) (2025, Schwensen·Rand·Smed) found that SCT reaches 33% of Zambia's population but was insufficient to offset rising national poverty, and assessed that the benefit amount corresponds to a purchasing power of $0.25 per household per day. The same evaluation recorded irregular disbursements and low benefit amounts as remaining challenges and urban targeting as a weak spot.

The UNU-WIDER Policy Brief (November 2021, Gasior et al.) estimated that under the MicroZAMOD model, the existing social protection system covers 76% of the extremely poor, but only 34% of the extremely poor receive SCT. The poverty reduction effect of the current system was 4%p overall (6%p in the group where additional programs were implemented), and the urban extremely poor emerged as the least supported group.

Representative Policy — Basic Education Assistance Module (BEAM) tuition support and Integrated Social Cash Transfer (ISCT)

Regarding the Basic Education Assistance Module (BEAM), which covers the tuition and examination fees of disadvantaged students paid by the government, Minister of Public Service, Labour, and Social Welfare July Moyo stated in parliament in 2024 that as of early 2023, ZW$199 billion in local currency had been partially disbursed for the tuition of 434,705 primary school students, but secondary schools were not paid, and schools denominated in US dollars did not receive funding. According to reports, as of 2023, the government's unpaid BEAM amount for primary and secondary schools was US$56.7 million (special schools separately at US$83,825), and a US$6.4 million debt default to the Zimbabwe School Examinations Council (ZIMSEC) made the 2024 final exam participation of the 532,000 BEAM recipients uncertain.

According to UNICEF, in August 2020 the Ministry of Public Service, Labour, and Social Welfare and UNICEF introduced an Emergency Social Cash Transfer (ESCT) targeting chronically vulnerable households in urban areas with funding from Germany and Sweden, designed to be integrated with the government-led Integrated Social Cash Transfer (ISCT). As of October 2022, ESCT provided monthly cash to over 25,000 households and 113,500 individuals (approximately 53,000 children) in urban areas of eight districts including Harare and Bulawayo, and the government took over 6,778 households in two districts, Gutu and Highfields, under ISCT.

The HSCT process evaluation (2014) conducted by the American Institutes for Research (AIR) and the University of North Carolina (UNC) research team described the program as targeting households with labor constraints and food poverty nationwide, and presented key recommendations to enhance staff and beneficiary community understanding of the program, revise communication strategies, strengthen monitoring and accountability structures, and harmonize with existing support programs. The literature analysis paper by Zimbabwean researchers (Chikoko et al., 2021) assessed that HSCT raised resilience and welfare among peripheral groups while also examining operational challenges.

Part 7 Limitations and Caveats

  1. Indicator years vary by country (latest values after 2010). Comparisons are not across the same year.
  2. For R1's ASPIRE, many high-income countries remain un-surveyed, so those countries' R1 is determined solely by SDG 1.3.1.
  3. SDG 1.3.1 and ASPIRE measure 'take-up'; they do not assess the adequacy of benefit levels.
  4. R4 (SWIID) is an estimate; countries with sparse raw data have high uncertainty.
  5. Published figures are as released by each country or institution. Overstating or omitting may occur; in cases, independent sources are presented side-by-side.

Anomalies and peculiarities discovered during the work were recorded in internal institute records (nci/anomalies_record.md) and will be addressed in the engine refinement phase.

Related Research — Papers and Reports

Academic papers, monographs, and international organization reports on the four axes of the National Capacity Index and the question 'Does policy reach the grassroots?'. All items were verified against the publisher/DOI pages for bibliographic details.

State Capacity and Policy Implementation

  1. Mann, M. (1984). The autonomous power of the state: its origins, mechanisms and results. European Journal of Sociology 25(2): 185–213. Academic Paper https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003975600004239
    The original text introducing the concept of 'substantive power'—the idea that states actually penetrate society across their territories to implement policies—which serves as the theoretical starting point for NCI's concept of policy 'reach'.
  2. Soifer, H. (2008). State Infrastructural Power: Approaches to Conceptualization and Measurement. Studies in Comparative International Development 43(3–4): 231–251. Academic Paper https://doi.org/10.1007/s12116-008-9028-6
    A paper summarizing methods to measure the effects of substructural power on state capacity, territorial disparities, and society, serving as the basis for designing NCI's four axes as outcome-based indicators.
  3. Besley, T. & Persson, T. (2011). Pillars of Prosperity: The Political Economics of Development Clusters. Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press. Monograph https://doi.org/10.23943/princeton/9780691152684.001.0001
    A work theorizing the structure in which fiscal and legal capacities co-evolve, providing the background for interpreting how redistribution through taxation and transfers (R4) and social protection reach (R1) move alongside state capacity.
  4. Andrews, M., Pritchett, L. & Woolcock, M. (2013). Escaping Capability Traps Through Problem Driven Iterative Adaptation (PDIA). World Development 51: 234–244. Academic Paper https://doi.org/10.1016/j.worlddev.2013.05.011
    A paper addressing the 'trap of capacity'—where institutions have formal structures (laws and programs) but lack the actual implementation capacity—which supports the design logic of NCI, which measures outcomes for low-income recipients rather than mere institutional possession.
  5. Lipsky, M. (2010). Street-Level Bureaucracy: Dilemmas of the Individual in Public Service (30th Anniversary Expanded Edition). New York: Russell Sage Foundation. Monograph https://muse.jhu.edu/book/15024
    A classic analyzing how policies are transmitted to actual beneficiaries by front-line bureaucrats under discretion and resource constraints, used to interpret the gap between designed benefits and actual reach (R1·R2).

R1 Income Security Reach — Social Protection Coverage, Targeting, and Non-Take-Up

  1. Coady, D., Grosh, M. & Hoddinott, J. (2004). Targeting Outcomes Redux. The World Bank Research Observer 19(1): 61–85. Academic Paper https://doi.org/10.1093/wbro/lkh016
    A meta-analysis comparing the performance of 122 poverty-targeted programs in 48 countries, showing that lower-quintile social protection coverage (R1) varies significantly by targeting method.
  2. Devereux, S., Masset, E., Sabates-Wheeler, R., Samson, M., Rivas, A.-M. & te Lintelo, D. (2017). The targeting effectiveness of social transfers. Journal of Development Effectiveness 9(2): 162–211. Academic Paper https://doi.org/10.1080/19439342.2017.1305981
    A paper systematically reviewing inclusion and exclusion errors in social transfer targeting, serving as the basis for interpreting why the poorest quintile coverage appears low in R1 (exclusion error).
  3. Currie, J. (2004). The Take Up of Social Benefits. NBER Working Paper No. 10488. Cambridge, MA: National Bureau of Economic Research. Academic Paper https://doi.org/10.3386/w10488
    A seminal literature that compiles the causes of 'non-take-up'—where eligible individuals do not receive benefits (information, stigma, administrative costs)—explaining the gap between institutional existence and actual reach.
  4. Eurofound (2015). Access to social benefits: Reducing non-take-up. Luxembourg: Publications Office of the European Union. International Organization Report https://www.eurofound.europa.eu/en/publications/all/access-social-benefits-reducing-non-take
    A report summarizing the gap between eligibility and actual take-up and the effects of simplified application procedures in 10 EU countries, demonstrating why R1 reach is incomplete even in high-income countries.
  5. International Labour Organization (2024). World Social Protection Report 2024–26: Universal social protection for climate action and a just transition. Geneva: ILO. International Organization Report https://doi.org/10.54394/ZMDK5543
    The official source for SDG 1.3.1 (social protection coverage) aggregation, serving as the country-level coverage data and defining literature for NCI's R1 axis.
  6. World Bank (2018). The State of Social Safety Nets 2018. Washington, DC: World Bank. International Organization Report https://doi.org/10.1596/978-1-4648-1254-5
    A report presenting social safety net coverage and beneficiary distribution by income quintile based on the ASPIRE database, serving as the source of R1's 'coverage rate of the poorest 20%' indicator.

R2 Basic Service Reach — Universal Health Coverage and Financial Protection

  1. Wagstaff, A., Flores, G., Hsu, J., Smitz, M.-F., Chepynoga, K., Buisman, L. R., van Wilgenburg, K. & Eozenou, P. (2018). Progress on catastrophic health spending in 133 countries: a retrospective observational study. The Lancet Global Health 6(2): e169–e179. Academic Paper https://doi.org/10.1016/S2214-109X(17)30429-1
    A paper estimating the incidence of catastrophic health expenditure using household surveys from 133 countries, serving as a methodological benchmark for interpreting R2's financial protection (SDG 3.8.2) indicator.
  2. World Health Organization & World Bank (2023). Tracking Universal Health Coverage: 2023 Global Monitoring Report. Geneva: WHO; Washington, DC: World Bank. International Organization Report https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240080379
    Official monitoring reports on the UHC service coverage index (SDG 3.8.1) and catastrophic health expenditure (SDG 3.8.2), serving as direct sources of R2 axis data.

R3 Opportunity Reach — Financial Inclusion · Educational Equity

  1. Demirgüç-Kunt, A., Klapper, L., Singer, D. & Ansar, S. (2022). The Global Findex Database 2021: Financial Inclusion, Digital Payments, and Resilience in the Age of COVID-19. Washington, DC: World Bank. International Organization Report https://doi.org/10.1596/978-1-4648-1897-4
    A database report providing financial inclusion indicators, such as account ownership rates among the bottom 40% of adults, by country, serving as the source of R3 financial inclusion indicators.
  2. Klapper, L., Singer, D., Starita, L. & Norris, A. (2025). The Global Findex Database 2025: Connectivity and Financial Inclusion in the Digital Economy. Washington, DC: World Bank. International Organization Report https://doi.org/10.1596/978-1-4648-2204-9
    The latest edition of Findex, which jointly addresses digital connectivity and the financial inclusion of the bottom 40%, serving as the reference data for updating R3 indicators to the latest year.
  3. UNESCO (2020). Global Education Monitoring Report 2020: Inclusion and education – All means all. Paris: UNESCO. International Organization Report https://www.unesco.org/gem-report/en/inclusion
    A report systematically addressing education access and completion gaps by wealth quintiles (parity index), serving as the basis for interpreting R3's educational wealth parity indicator.

R4 Redistributive Reach — Fiscal Attribution · Income Distribution

  1. Lustig, N. (Ed.) (2022). Commitment to Equity Handbook: Estimating the Impact of Fiscal Policy on Inequality and Poverty (2nd ed., 2 vols.). Washington, DC: Brookings Institution Press. Monograph https://www.brookings.edu/books/commitment-to-equity-handbook
    The standard textbook of the fiscal attribution (CEQ) methodology, which measures the effects of taxes, transfers, and in-kind benefits on inequality and poverty, serving as the conceptual basis for R4 redistribution indicators.
  2. Solt, F. (2020). Measuring Income Inequality Across Countries and Over Time: The Standardized World Income Inequality Database. Social Science Quarterly 101(3): 1183–1199. Academic Paper https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.12795
    An explanatory paper for the SWIID that standardizes market income Gini and disposable income Gini for cross-country comparison, serving as the source data for calculating 'the reduction in Gini through taxes and transfers' in R4.
